passed.title: Pass maintain_order=True when the order of unique values matters
passed.trap: `Series.unique` defaults to `maintain_order=False`, so the order of the result is not guaranteed. Code that takes the first unique value, or that zips the result with something else, can silently change between runs. Pass `maintain_order=True` to keep first-appearance order, or call `Series.sort` on the result if you want sorted order.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series('a', [3, 1, 3, 2])

# Default: order is not guaranteed, so sort explicitly if you need a stable result
print(s.unique().sort().to_list())

# First-appearance order, like pandas unique()
print(s.unique(maintain_order=True).to_list())

passed.title: Sort the result of top_k yourself and expect nulls to be skipped
passed.trap: `Series.top_k` and `Series.top_k_by` do not return elements in any particular order. Do not assume the first element is the largest; call `Series.sort` on the result. Non-null elements are always preferred over nulls, and for `Series.top_k_by` this holds regardless of `reverse`. So a 'smallest k' query with `reverse=True` picks non-null values before any nulls rather than treating null as the minimum.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series('a', [2, None, 5, 1, 4])

# Unordered output: sort explicitly
print(s.top_k(3).sort(descending=True).to_list())

# reverse=True gives the smallest values, and nulls are still skipped
print(s.top_k_by('a', 2, reverse=True).sort().to_list())

passed.title: Series.var uses the sample variance (ddof=1) by default
passed.trap: `Series.var` divides by `N - ddof` with `ddof=1` by default, which gives the sample variance. Code ported from NumPy, where the default is population variance (`ddof=0`), will get different numbers. Pass `ddof=0` explicitly when you want the population variance.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series('a', [1, 2, 3])
print(s.var())        # sample variance, ddof=1
print(s.var(ddof=0))  # population variance

passed.title: to_physical output depends on dtype details and is not a stable encoding
passed.trap: `Series.to_physical` exposes the internal representation. For example, `Datetime` becomes `Int64` counted in the column's own time unit, so the same instant gives different integers for `ms` and `us`. `Categorical` becomes `UInt32` codes. The docs warn that physical representations are an implementation detail and not guaranteed to be stable, so do not persist or compare these integers across datasets. For epoch values with an explicit unit, use `Expr.dt.epoch`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.select(
    ms=pl.datetime(2024, 1, 1, time_unit='ms'),
    us=pl.datetime(2024, 1, 1, time_unit='us'),
)
print(df['ms'].to_physical().to_list())
print(df['us'].to_physical().to_list())

# Explicit unit: identical regardless of storage unit
print(df.select(pl.col('ms', 'us').dt.epoch('s')).row(0))

passed.title: Pair unique_counts with unique(maintain_order=True), not the default unique
passed.trap: `Series.unique_counts` returns only the counts, in order of first appearance, and not the values. The default `Series.unique()` does not guarantee order, so zipping the two can attach counts to the wrong values. Pair it with `Series.unique(maintain_order=True)`, or use `Series.value_counts` to get values and counts together.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series('id', ['b', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'b'])
keys = s.unique(maintain_order=True)
counts = s.unique_counts()
print(list(zip(keys.to_list(), counts.to_list())))

vc = s.value_counts()
print(sorted(vc.rows()))

passed.title: value_counts returns an unsorted DataFrame with a 'count' column
passed.trap: `Series.value_counts` returns a `DataFrame` with one column of values and one column of counts. It does not return a Series indexed by value. The counts column is named `count`, or `proportion` when `normalize=True`. The default is `sort=False`, which leaves the row order non-deterministic, so `.head(1)` is not reliably the most frequent value. Pass `sort=True` for descending counts, and use `name=` to choose the count column name.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series('color', ['red', 'blue', 'red', 'green', 'blue', 'blue'])
vc = s.value_counts(sort=True)
print(isinstance(vc, pl.DataFrame), vc.columns)
print(vc.rows())
print(s.value_counts(sort=True, normalize=True).columns)
print(s.value_counts(sort=True, name='n').columns)

passed.title: zip_with keeps self where the mask is True and takes a Series for other
passed.trap: `Series.zip_with(mask, other)` takes values from `self` where `mask` is true and from `other` where it is false. The calling Series is the 'true' branch, so swapping `self` and `other` silently inverts the selection. `other` is documented as a Series of the same type, so pass a Series rather than a scalar. For conditional logic inside a frame, prefer `pl.when`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s1 = pl.Series('a', [1, 2, 3])
s2 = pl.Series('b', [10, 20, 30])
mask = pl.Series([True, False, True])
print(s1.zip_with(mask, s2).to_list())  # self where True
print(s2.zip_with(mask, s1).to_list())  # swapped: inverted selection

passed.title: to_numpy may return a read-only array, and zero_copy_only is deprecated
passed.trap: When the conversion is zero-copy (numeric dtype, no nulls, single chunk), `Series.to_numpy` returns an array that is not writable, and in-place assignment on it raises an error. Pass `writable=True` to force a copy you can mutate. The `zero_copy_only` parameter is deprecated in favour of `allow_copy=False`, which is its inverse, and `use_pyarrow` is deprecated as well. With `allow_copy=False`, any conversion that needs a copy fails, for example a Series with nulls.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series('a', [1, 2, 3], dtype=pl.Int8)
arr = s.to_numpy()
try:
    arr[0] = 10
except Exception as e:
    print(repr(e).split('(')[0])

w = s.to_numpy(writable=True)
w[0] = 10
print(pl.Series(w).to_list(), s.to_list())

try:
    pl.Series('b', [1, None]).to_numpy(allow_copy=False)
except Exception as e:
    print(repr(e).split('(')[0])
